item.title: £1.4bn investment portfolios available for sale
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New research from Rushbrook has revealed 1,322 property investment portfolios currently available for purchase across England, with a combined value exceeding £1.4 billion. The findings highlight significant opportunities for portfolio investors, particularly in the capital where London-based properties account for nearly a third of the total market value.

Regional Breakdown of Available Portfolios

The research provides a detailed geographical analysis of investment opportunities across England:

  • London represents the highest concentration by value, with portfolios worth approximately £460 million
  • The South East follows with around £320 million worth of portfolio listings
  • Northern regions collectively account for nearly £280 million of available investments
  • The Midlands offers portfolios valued at roughly £200 million

This distribution suggests that while London dominates in terms of individual property values, substantial investment potential exists throughout England. Property investors might consider regional variations in yields and capital growth prospects when evaluating these opportunities.

What Portfolio Investors Should Consider

For those contemplating purchasing a property portfolio, several factors could be worth evaluating:

  • Portfolio composition – whether it consists of residential, commercial or mixed property types
  • Current tenancy arrangements and rental income streams
  • Local market conditions in the portfolio's geographical area
  • Mortgage financing options for portfolio purchases
  • Potential for value-add through refurbishment or management improvements

Portfolio investors may wish to seek specialist mortgage advice, as financing multiple properties often involves different criteria compared to single buy-to-let purchases. Lenders typically assess the overall strength of the portfolio rather than individual properties when making lending decisions.

With £1.4 billion worth of portfolios currently on the market, investors have substantial choice across England. However, thorough due diligence remains essential when considering any property investment opportunity.

item.title: Widest gap between sales and listings in a year
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Recent market analysis reveals a growing disparity between property listings and completed sales across the UK, with conversion rates dropping to their lowest levels in twelve months. According to industry data, only 41.9% of available properties are currently progressing to sale completion, highlighting potential challenges in the current housing market.

Market dynamics show shifting trends

While the number of available properties on the market has increased, the rate at which these listings convert to sales has declined significantly. This divergence suggests that despite greater choice for prospective buyers, other factors may be influencing purchasing decisions. Market observers note this represents the widest gap between supply and demand witnessed since late 2022.

Several elements could be contributing to this trend, including economic uncertainty, mortgage rate fluctuations, and seasonal variations in buyer activity. The data indicates that homeowners looking to sell may need to adjust their expectations regarding timelines and pricing strategies in the current climate.

What this means for homeowners and buyers

For those considering entering the market, these figures present both opportunities and challenges. Buyers may find themselves with more negotiating power given the higher inventory levels, whilst sellers might need to adopt more competitive pricing approaches to secure interest.

  • Properties may remain on the market for longer periods before securing buyers
  • Sellers could need to be more flexible on pricing expectations
  • Buyers may have greater scope for negotiation on asking prices

The coming months will reveal whether this trend represents a temporary adjustment or a more sustained shift in market behaviour. Those monitoring the situation might wish to keep abreast of mortgage rate movements and broader economic indicators that could influence housing market dynamics.

item.title: Unpaid Invoices in Property: What Sourcers, Agents and Contractors Can Do When Clients Don’t Pay
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Unpaid invoices can pose significant challenges for professionals in the property sector, from contractors and tradespeople to letting agents and property sourcers. While completing a job to a high standard is satisfying, delayed or ignored payments can disrupt cash flow, hinder business growth, and even threaten survival. For those facing this issue, understanding the steps to address unpaid invoices can be crucial.

Why Unpaid Invoices Matter

For many property professionals, cash flow is the lifeblood of their business. Unpaid invoices can create a domino effect, impacting the ability to pay suppliers, cover overheads, or take on new projects. This is particularly true for smaller businesses or self-employed individuals who may not have substantial financial reserves. Addressing unpaid invoices promptly can help mitigate these risks and ensure smoother operations.

Steps to Take When Payments Are Delayed

When faced with unpaid invoices, there are several actions property professionals might consider. First, sending a polite reminder to the client can often resolve the issue. Many delays are unintentional, and a simple nudge may prompt payment. If this doesn’t work, issuing a formal letter outlining the outstanding amount and setting a clear deadline can be more effective.

For persistent non-payment, seeking legal advice or using a debt collection service could be necessary. In some cases, pursuing legal action through a small claims court might be the most appropriate course. While this can be time-consuming, it can also send a strong message to clients who repeatedly fail to meet payment obligations.

Preventing Future Payment Issues

Prevention is often better than cure when it comes to unpaid invoices. One approach is to implement clear payment terms from the outset, ensuring clients understand when and how payments are expected. Requesting deposits or staged payments for larger projects can also help maintain cash flow and reduce the risk of non-payment.

Using written contracts or agreements can provide additional protection, as they legally outline the scope of work and payment expectations. For those working with new or unfamiliar clients, conducting credit checks or requesting references may offer further reassurance.

Dealing with unpaid invoices can be stressful, but taking proactive steps can help property professionals safeguard their finances and maintain healthy business relationships. By addressing delays promptly and implementing preventative measures, sourcers, agents, contractors, and tradespeople can reduce the impact of non-payment and focus on growing their businesses.

item.title: Brickflow adds funding options to Upstix
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Property investors looking to streamline their funding options may benefit from a recent collaboration between Brickflow and Upstix. The partnership aims to simplify the process of securing finance by providing access to a wide range of lenders, potentially making property purchases more efficient for buyers.

A Wider Range of Funding Options

Brickflow, known for its innovative approach to property finance, has joined forces with Upstix to offer investors access to funding from over 160 lenders. This integration allows users to compare a variety of financial products, including bridging loans, buy-to-let mortgages, and development finance, all in one place. By consolidating these options, the partnership seeks to save time for property investors whilst ensuring they can make informed decisions about their funding needs.

Streamlining Property Purchases

The collaboration between Brickflow and Upstix is designed to simplify the property investment process. Investors can now use Upstix’s platform to access Brickflow’s extensive lender network, enabling them to secure finance more quickly and efficiently. This could be particularly valuable for those looking to capitalise on time-sensitive opportunities in the property market. Additionally, the streamlined process may reduce the administrative burden often associated with securing funding, allowing investors to focus on growing their portfolios.

Benefits for Investors

For property investors, the integration of Brickflow’s funding options into Upstix’s platform offers several potential advantages. Firstly, it provides access to a broader range of financial products, increasing the likelihood of finding a suitable deal. Secondly, the ability to compare multiple lenders in one place could help investors secure more competitive rates. Finally, the streamlined process may reduce delays, enabling investors to move swiftly on property purchases. This collaboration could prove particularly beneficial for those navigating complex or fast-moving transactions.

As the property market continues to evolve, tools like those offered by Brickflow and Upstix may become increasingly valuable for investors. By simplifying access to finance and reducing administrative hurdles, this partnership could help investors make more informed and timely decisions, potentially enhancing their overall investment strategy.

item.title: Lendlord launches new register tool
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A new digital tool designed to simplify landlord registration in England has been launched by property management platform Lendlord. The service aims to assist buy-to-let investors in preparing for upcoming regulatory changes whilst maintaining ongoing compliance with rental property requirements.

Streamlining landlord registration

With England's property registration scheme expected to roll out in 2025, many landlords face new administrative responsibilities. Lendlord's tool provides a centralised platform to manage documentation, track deadlines and maintain up-to-date records for multiple rental properties. The system automatically flags when renewals or updates are required, potentially helping landlords avoid costly compliance oversights.

Key features include:

  • Automated alerts for registration renewals
  • Centralised document storage for property portfolios
  • Step-by-step guidance through application processes
  • Compliance checklists tailored to local authority requirements

Preparing for regulatory changes

The launch coincides with government plans to introduce a national landlord register in England, similar to schemes already operating in Scotland and Wales. While full details remain under consultation, the database will likely require landlords to provide property details, safety certificates and ownership documentation.

Industry experts suggest the private rental sector faces increasing regulation, with landlords needing to demonstrate compliance across multiple areas including:

  • Energy Performance Certificate ratings
  • Gas and electrical safety certificates
  • Deposit protection schemes
  • Right to Rent immigration checks

Property owners with multiple buy-to-let investments might particularly benefit from digital management tools as regulatory requirements become more complex. Lendlord's platform joins several emerging solutions designed to help landlords navigate the changing compliance landscape without professional property management services.

As rental sector regulations continue evolving, staying informed about new requirements remains crucial for landlords. Digital tools can offer practical support, though specialist legal advice may still be necessary for complex cases or portfolio management.

item.title: Home movers turn against government as Budget fears mount
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

With the Budget looming next week, new research reveals growing dissatisfaction among UK home movers regarding government housing policies. According to OnTheMarket's latest Property Sentiment Index, 43% of active buyers believe recent government measures have negatively impacted the property market, while just 21% feel they've been beneficial. This discontent comes alongside rising concerns about potential interest rate increases in the coming months.

Buyer confidence persists despite mortgage concerns

The survey of over 6,400 respondents conducted in September shows a resilient property market, with 89% of active buyers confident about securing funds for their next home purchase – a figure unchanged since May. This suggests that whilst borrowers are increasingly wary of higher borrowing costs, most are adjusting their plans rather than abandoning them altogether.

Expectations around interest rates have shifted significantly, with 41% of active movers now anticipating rate rises in the next six months, compared to 29% in the previous quarter. Among the general public, 44% predict increases, up from 34% previously. Only 8% of active movers expect rates to fall, indicating widespread caution about future mortgage costs.

Mixed signals for property prices and government policy

Despite these concerns, there are tentative signs of improving sentiment towards house prices. A third of respondents (33%) now expect property values to rise over the next 12 months, up from 31% - the first annual increase in this measure. Renters also show relative optimism, with 87% confident about finding a property within six months.

The dissatisfaction with government housing policy extends beyond active movers, with 35% of the general public believing recent measures have damaged the property market versus just 9% who think they've helped. This growing discontent comes as the Chancellor prepares to deliver what many hope will be a housing-focused Budget.

Calls for government action

Jason Tebb, president of OnTheMarket, has urged the government to use the Budget to address these concerns: "Home movers are currently operating with one hand tied behind their back. The significant disparity between those who feel government policy has harmed versus helped the market, coupled with heightened interest rate expectations, creates unnecessary hurdles."

Tebb warned that prolonged uncertainty could eventually erode the current market confidence. As buyers and sellers navigate these challenging conditions, many will be watching next week's Budget announcements closely for measures that could ease pressure on the housing market.

item.title: AI moves deeper into property sector as mortgage advisers embrace automation
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK mortgage sector is witnessing a significant shift as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in day-to-day operations. Mortgage advisers are now adopting specialised AI tools that integrate directly with their customer relationship management (CRM) systems, aiming to streamline administrative processes whilst maintaining regulatory compliance.

AI integration transforms mortgage advice

A new partnership between AI specialist PlannerPal and mortgage technology provider Twenty7Tec has brought automated solutions to the ADVICE CRM platform. This development allows brokers to record client conversations, generate meeting notes and prepare documentation without leaving their primary work system. Financial advice firms already using this technology reportedly manage over £150 billion in client assets collectively, with the mortgage sector now following suit.

Early adopters like London-based Charles Cameron & Associates, part of Amber River Group, report rapid adoption among their 130-strong adviser team. Within three weeks of implementation, over 90% of advisers were actively using the AI assistant. The firm highlights how the technology adapts to natural advisory conversations rather than imposing scripted interactions, helping maintain consistent documentation standards across all client cases.

Balancing automation with professional oversight

While embracing these productivity tools, mortgage advisory firms are taking a measured approach to AI implementation. Many are choosing specialised financial services solutions over generic AI tools, allowing customisation to their specific compliance requirements and working practices.

Notably, the human element remains central to the advice process. Advisers retain responsibility for reviewing all AI-generated content before it enters client records, ensuring accuracy and maintaining regulatory standards. This hybrid approach aims to combine the efficiency gains of automation with the irreplaceable expertise of qualified professionals.

The mortgage sector's adoption of AI mirrors broader trends across the property industry, where estate agency software providers have similarly introduced automation features to reduce administrative burdens. As these technologies mature, homeowners might notice quicker response times and more standardised documentation throughout their property transactions.

For borrowers, these developments could translate to more efficient mortgage application processes in the long term, though the fundamental importance of personalised financial advice remains unchanged. As with any financial decision, consulting a qualified mortgage adviser continues to be essential when navigating the housing market.

item.title: Rightmove hit by major Google Cloud outage as websites go down
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A widespread Google Cloud outage disrupted Rightmove and other key online services on Tuesday, temporarily affecting property searches and estate agent operations across the UK. The incident stemmed from power failures at Google's London data centres, with most services restored by mid-afternoon. Rightmove confirmed its platform returned to normal operation following what it described as temporary "technical issues" affecting logged-in users.

How the outage affected property searches

The technical problems raised concerns for estate and letting agents relying on Rightmove for property marketing. During the disruption, prospective buyers and tenants might have experienced difficulties accessing listings or submitting enquiries through the platform. While Rightmove hasn't disclosed specific figures regarding impacted users, the incident serves as a reminder of how digital platforms underpin modern property transactions.

Homeowners and property seekers might wish to consider having alternative property portals bookmarked in case of future technical issues. Most major high street agents list properties across multiple platforms, so checking an agent's own website could provide backup access to listings during outages.

Broader impact of cloud service disruptions

The Google Cloud incident affected numerous UK services beyond the property sector, including several banking platforms, delivery services and even NHS digital systems. This highlights how many organisations now depend on cloud infrastructure providers for critical operations. When these systems experience problems, the effects can ripple across unrelated industries simultaneously.

For businesses considering their technology infrastructure, the outage demonstrates the importance of:

  • Understanding service level agreements with cloud providers
  • Having contingency plans for technical failures
  • Considering multi-cloud or hybrid infrastructure approaches

While cloud computing offers significant advantages for scalability and cost-efficiency, Tuesday's events show that even industry leaders like Google can experience unexpected downtime. Businesses may wish to review their reliance on single providers for mission-critical operations.

As digital services become increasingly central to property transactions and other sectors, both businesses and consumers might consider how they would adapt during unexpected technical outages. Having offline contact details for important services and alternative access methods could prove valuable during such disruptions.

item.title: AI is changing the way consumers complain, but is it making their complaints stronger?
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the way consumers lodge complaints, particularly in the property and mortgage sectors. What was once a simple email detailing a grievance may now arrive as a highly detailed, structured argument, packed with technical jargon and legal references. Whilst AI can be a useful tool for consumers, it is also reshaping the nature of complaints, making them more complex for agents and professionals to navigate.

The Rise of AI-Assisted Complaints

Reports suggest that around 85% of consumer complaints now involve some element of AI assistance. Homeowners and buyers often turn to AI to help them understand whether their experience is reasonable, what industry best practice looks like, or whether something has gone wrong. For those unfamiliar with the intricacies of the property market, AI can be a valuable resource in articulating concerns. However, it can also complicate matters by identifying every possible issue, even those that may not be relevant to the situation at hand.

Whilst AI can simplify complex scenarios, it does not always discern which points are crucial or how expectations should be managed. This can lead to complaints that are far more detailed and technical than necessary, often losing the emotional nuance that typically accompanies human-written grievances. For property professionals, this means spending additional time unpicking lengthy arguments to identify the core issue.

The Challenges for Property Professionals

The increasing use of AI in complaints presents several challenges for agents and redress schemes. Complaints are becoming more structured and formal, but this does not always equate to accuracy or relevance. For example, a consumer might cite obscure legal terms or raise multiple issues that complicate the resolution process. Whilst these complaints may appear well-researched, they can sometimes obscure the actual problem.

Moreover, AI-generated complaints often lack the personal touch that helps agents understand the consumer’s perspective. This can make it harder to empathise and find a swift resolution. Additionally, the uniformity of AI-generated content means complaints can start to sound repetitive, making it more difficult to address each case uniquely.

Embracing AI in the Complaints Process

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Lomond, one of the UK’s leading estate agency groups, has announced the appointment of two senior executives as part of its ongoing expansion strategy. Darrell Evans joins as chief commercial officer, whilst Steve Maddock takes on the role of chief operating officer. These appointments follow a series of acquisitions by Lomond, including Ocean in Bristol, FHP Living in Nottingham, and City Residential in Liverpool.

Darrell Evans: A Wealth of Experience

Darrell Evans brings over three decades of experience in financial services and commercial leadership to Lomond. In his new role, he will oversee the group’s commercial strategy, revenue growth, marketing, and lead generation. Additionally, he will take responsibility for Lomond Investment Management (LIM). Evans has held prominent roles in the past, including chief executive of Benenden Health and chief commercial officer at the Co-operative Bank. His career also includes positions at RBS, Direct Line Group, and Virgin Money, making him a seasoned professional in the industry.

Evans expressed his enthusiasm for joining Lomond, stating: “Lomond has established a unique position within the UK property sector, and the ambition to deliver outstanding experiences for its customers is one I’m excited to foster and expand upon.”

Steve Maddock: Operational Expertise

Steve Maddock, meanwhile, will focus on Lomond’s operations and technology functions. With more than 30 years of experience in operational management and business transformation, Maddock is well-equipped to drive the group’s efficiency and growth. He spent 11 years at Direct Line, including six as chief operating officer, where he worked alongside Lomond’s current chief executive, Paul Geddes. Maddock also served as chair of the Motor Insurers’ Bureau for seven years, further solidifying his credentials.

Maddock commented on his appointment: “Lomond already has an exceptionally strong foundation in place, and there’s a clear opportunity to build on it ahead. I’m thoroughly looking forward to working alongside Darrell, Paul, and the wider leadership team to power Lomond in this next stage of growth.”

Partridge Homes Expands Lettings Team

In related news, Partridge Homes, a Birmingham-based estate agency, has expanded its lettings team following its strongest year for new rental agreements since its inception in 2007. The family-run business has appointed Katie Fisher as property manager, marking its third lettings appointment since May. This expansion comes after Partridge Homes agreed to almost 40 new tenancies in September alone, highlighting its growing presence in the rental market.

These developments underscore the dynamic nature of the UK property sector, with both Lomond and Partridge Homes making strategic moves to strengthen their positions in the market. For homeowners and landlords alike, these changes could signal new opportunities and enhanced services in the months ahead.

item.title: Franchisees acquire 25-year-old estate agency
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Open House franchisees have completed their first acquisition under the company's Assisted Acquisitions Programme, marking a significant milestone for the expanding network. Kane and Debi Platt, who operate Open House Warrington, have taken ownership of long-established estate agency Halton Kelly – a business with over 25 years of trading history in the local property market.

Franchise Network Expansion

The acquisition represents the first completed deal under Open House's new growth strategy following its takeover by Sourced Property Group earlier this year. The programme aims to help franchisees expand their operations by acquiring established estate agencies and lettings businesses across the UK. The Warrington-based Halton Kelly will now trade as "Halton Kelly, powered by Open House", maintaining its local identity while benefiting from national network support.

Stephen Moss, CEO of Sourced Property Group, commented: "This creates a new growth path for ambitious franchisees while giving existing agency owners options for their business succession plans. The model provides continuity for clients while bringing fresh ambition to established local brands."

Blending Local Expertise with National Support

The new owners have emphasised their commitment to maintaining the agency's local roots while leveraging the advantages of being part of a national franchise. Debi Platt explained: "We're keeping the personal service and community knowledge clients value, while gaining access to wider resources and expertise. Our focus remains on serving Warrington's property market with local decision-making."

Previous owner Simon Kelly will remain actively involved in the business, ensuring a smooth transition for staff and clients. Industry observers note this acquisition model could appeal to independent agents considering succession options while wanting to maintain local market presence.

The property sector will watch with interest as Open House pursues further acquisitions under this programme, potentially reshaping how franchise networks expand their UK footprint. For homeowners in Warrington, the change brings the promise of continued local service with enhanced resources behind the scenes.

item.title: Location, location, education: School house price premium falls
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Families looking to settle near top-performing secondary schools in England have traditionally faced a steep premium when buying property. However, new research suggests this premium is beginning to shrink, offering some potential relief for parents prioritising education in their house hunt.

The Price of Education

According to a recent study by Savills, homes in constituencies with the highest-performing secondary schools cost an average of £645,601, which is 29% above their respective regional averages. Detached homes in these areas command an even greater premium, averaging £1.41m – a staggering 56% above regional benchmarks. Despite these figures, the premium has actually decreased over the past decade, falling from 33% ten years ago to 29% today.

The research analysed house prices and GCSE Attainment 8 scores across 543 parliamentary constituencies in England. Richmond Park emerged as the top performer, with an average score of 64.7 and an average house price of £1,059,496 – 54% above the London average. Altrincham and Sale West ranked second, with an average score of 61.4 and property prices of £557,947, more than double the North West regional average.

Exceptions to the Rule

Interestingly, the study also revealed that not all areas with strong schools come with sky-high property prices. For instance, Carshalton and Wallington, which ranks ninth nationally, has an average property cost of £491,271 – 29% below the London average. Similarly, Sutton and Cheam, ranked seventh, offers an average house price of £515,839, representing a 25% discount compared to the London average.

These findings highlight the nuances in the relationship between school performance and property prices. Whilst many areas with top schools command a premium, there are exceptions where families can access excellent education without the hefty price tag.

Slower Growth in Top School Areas

Another notable trend is the slower house price growth in areas with the strongest-performing schools. Over the past decade, these areas have seen some of the weakest growth in property values. This has contributed to the shrinking premium, making it slightly more affordable for families to move into these sought-after locations.

For example, whilst Richmond Park boasts the highest average Attainment 8 score, its house price growth has not kept pace with other areas. Similarly, Altrincham and Sale West, despite their strong educational credentials, have not experienced the same level of property value increases as other parts of the North West.

For homeowners considering a move to a top-performing school area, these trends could offer a window of opportunity. However, it remains essential to weigh up the costs and benefits carefully, as the premium – although shrinking – is still significant in many areas.

item.title: Speed Over Rate: Why Experienced Portfolio Investors Think About Finance Differently
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

When it comes to property investment, seasoned portfolio landlords often prioritise different mortgage factors compared to those just starting out. While new investors may focus solely on securing the lowest interest rate, experienced investors with multiple properties frequently value speed and flexibility above all else.

The Speed Versus Rate Trade-Off

For landlords managing extensive property portfolios, the ability to move quickly on new opportunities can outweigh marginal differences in interest rates. A slightly higher-rate mortgage that completes within weeks rather than months might represent better value when properties are in high demand. This approach acknowledges that delayed financing could mean missing out on prime investments altogether.

Several factors contribute to this mindset among portfolio landlords:

  • Competition for high-yielding properties in sought-after locations
  • The need to complete before competing buyers
  • The financial impact of void periods when waiting for finance
  • Opportunity costs of delayed investment decisions

Specialist Lending Solutions

Many portfolio investors turn to specialist lenders who understand the need for swift transactions. While these products might carry slightly higher rates than standard buy-to-let mortgages, they often offer:

  • Faster application processing times
  • More flexible underwriting criteria
  • Higher loan-to-value ratios for portfolio cases
  • Bespoke lending solutions for complex scenarios

Some specialist lenders have dedicated teams for portfolio landlords, streamlining the approval process while maintaining robust credit checks. This balance between speed and responsible lending makes them particularly attractive to experienced investors.

For investors considering this approach, it could be worth discussing options with a whole-of-market mortgage broker who understands both mainstream and specialist lending markets. They can help weigh up whether a potentially higher-rate mortgage with faster completion might better serve long-term portfolio growth objectives.

item.title: Commonhold reforms face major practical hurdles, property experts warn
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Property experts have raised significant concerns over the practical implementation of the government's proposed commonhold reforms, highlighting potential hurdles around mortgage lending, management costs and conversion processes. The warnings emerged during discussions at the recent Association of Leasehold Enfranchisement Practitioners (ALEP) conference, where industry professionals examined the draft Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill.

Mortgage lending and conversion costs raise concerns

The government's plans to make commonhold the default tenure for new flats and simplify conversions for existing leaseholders face several financial challenges. Industry professionals noted that unclear funding mechanisms for conversions could create barriers, particularly when some leaseholders may struggle to contribute financially. The treatment of existing mortgages under the new system also requires clarification to maintain lender confidence.

Mark Chick, director at ALEP, emphasised that successful reform would require coordinated preparation across the property sector. This includes establishing robust systems for property registration, mortgage provision and ongoing financial management. Lenders will need assurance that commonhold properties offer sufficient security before offering mortgage products, while residents taking control of buildings must fully understand their financial responsibilities.

Management responsibilities under commonhold

Delegates at the conference highlighted that building maintenance obligations remain unchanged regardless of ownership structure. Commonhold associations will need to establish effective systems for collecting contributions, maintaining reserve funds and handling day-to-day management. The reforms must address how these associations will enforce payment collection and ensure buildings meet all safety and regulatory requirements.

The discussions also covered how the proposed commonhold system would interact with provisions from the Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act 2024. Contributions from representatives across the sector, including major lenders and property firms, examined practical considerations around valuations, collective enfranchisement and recent legal developments.

While the move towards commonhold aims to give homeowners greater control, industry experts stress that successful implementation will depend on addressing these practical challenges. The government will need to work closely with lenders, managing agents and legal professionals to create a system that works for all stakeholders while protecting homeowners' interests.

item.title: Rogue agents exposed in BBC investigation
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A recent BBC Panorama investigation has brought to light concerning practices within the UK’s supported exempt accommodation (SEA) sector, raising questions about the exploitation of vulnerable tenants and potential misuse of housing benefits. The programme, which aired on BBC One and is available on BBC iPlayer, highlighted allegations of inadequate tenant support, suspected benefit fraud, and instances where housing benefit claims were made for individuals who were not residing in the properties.

Supported exempt accommodation is designed to house vulnerable groups, including domestic abuse survivors, former prisoners, and those recovering from addiction. In Birmingham alone, the Department for Work and Pensions allocated £410 million to SEA in the last financial year, with over 34,000 individuals living in such properties across the city. However, the investigation suggests that some managing agents may be prioritising profits over the welfare of tenants.

Concerns Over Tenant Support

The Panorama team focused on Second City Support Ltd, a managing agent overseeing a Birmingham property on behalf of Dawson Housing. Dawson Housing received £443 per week in housing benefit for one tenant, Alysha, who had sought refuge from domestic abuse. Alysha claimed she received minimal support and endured an eight-day period without heating or hot water. While Dawson Housing disputed these allegations, citing regular face-to-face assistance, their lawyers acknowledged some communication issues but denied any prolonged heating outage.

In addition to concerns over tenant support, the investigation raised questions about the financial practices of some managing agents. Darren Davey, owner of Second City Housing Properties and other companies, came under scrutiny. Land Registry records revealed that one property managed by his company was purchased for £191,000 in 2024 and sold for £410,000 just a year later. Davey explained that significant renovation costs justified the sale price, but BBC analysis also showed he received £2.9 million in dividends and over £900,000 in salary across three financial years. Davey emphasised that these earnings were linked to his broader business interests, not solely supported accommodation.

Ghost Tenants and Benefit Fraud

Perhaps the most alarming discovery was the alleged practice of using “ghost tenants” to claim housing benefits. Panorama uncovered advertisements on social media platforms, including Facebook, seeking individuals whose details could be used to support benefit claims without them actually occupying the properties. Such practices, if proven, would constitute serious fraud and undermine the integrity of the housing benefit system.

The investigation also highlighted how some managing agents have used incentives like free rooms, games consoles, and even holidays to attract tenants. While these offers may appear appealing, they raise ethical concerns about the motivations behind them and the potential exploitation of vulnerable individuals.

As the findings of the Panorama investigation continue to spark debate, homeowners and tenants alike may wish to remain vigilant about the practices of managing agents and housing providers. For those navigating the SEA sector, understanding their rights and seeking independent advice could prove invaluable in ensuring fair treatment and support.

item.title: Chancellor rules out capital gains tax rise ahead of Budget
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Property investors and second-home owners can breathe a sigh of relief as Chancellor John Healey confirms Capital Gains Tax (CGT) rates will remain unchanged in next week’s Budget. The decision follows speculation that the Treasury might align CGT with income tax rates, which could have significantly increased tax liabilities for landlords and property sellers.

Stability for property investors

The Chancellor’s confirmation maintains the current CGT structure, where higher-rate taxpayers face a 24% rate on residential property gains, while basic-rate taxpayers typically pay 18%. These rates remain considerably lower than the 45% additional income tax rate applied in most of the UK.

Property professionals have welcomed the decision, noting that stable CGT rates provide clarity for:

  • Buy-to-let landlords considering portfolio adjustments
  • Owners of second homes contemplating sales
  • Property investors making long-term financial plans

Some experts suggest the move may encourage more property transactions in the coming months, as sellers no longer face the prospect of imminent tax increases on their capital gains.

Economic considerations behind the decision

Treasury analysis reportedly influenced the Chancellor’s decision, with officials warning that higher CGT rates could backfire economically. Research indicates that increasing the higher CGT rate by 10 percentage points might actually reduce government revenues by approximately £3.6 billion by 2028-29.

Key concerns included:

  • The potential for investors to delay property sales indefinitely
  • The risk of wealthy individuals relocating overseas
  • Negative impacts on business investment confidence

Former Goldman Sachs chief economist Lord Jim O’Neill publicly opposed CGT increases, arguing they would send damaging signals to the business community during a period of economic uncertainty.

Looking ahead to Budget announcements

While the CGT decision provides certainty in one area, property owners should remain alert for other potential tax changes when the Chancellor delivers his Budget on 28 October. The Treasury may still introduce adjustments to property taxation through alternative measures.

Financial advisers recommend that landlords and investors review their portfolios in light of the confirmed CGT position, as those considering property sales might find the current tax regime more favourable than potential future changes. As always, seeking professional tax advice tailored to individual circumstances remains crucial when making significant financial decisions.

The Chancellor’s confirmation maintains the current CGT structure, where higher-rate taxpayers face a 24% rate on residential property gains, while basic-rate taxpayers typically pay 18%. These rates remain considerably lower than the 45% additional income tax rate applied in most of the UK.

Property professionals have welcomed the decision, noting that stable CGT rates provide clarity for:

  • Buy-to-let landlords considering portfolio adjustments
  • Owners of second homes contemplating sales
  • Property investors making long-term financial plans

Some experts suggest the move may encourage more property transactions in the coming months, as sellers no longer face the prospect of imminent tax increases on their capital gains.

Economic considerations behind the decision

Treasury analysis reportedly influenced the Chancellor’s decision, with officials warning that higher CGT rates could backfire economically. Research indicates that increasing the higher CGT rate by 10 percentage points might actually reduce government revenues by approximately £3.6 billion by 2028-29.

Key concerns included:

  • The potential for investors to delay property sales indefinitely
  • The risk of wealthy individuals relocating overseas
  • Negative impacts on business investment confidence

Former Goldman Sachs chief economist Lord Jim O’Neill publicly opposed CGT increases, arguing they would send damaging signals to the business community during a period of economic uncertainty.

Looking ahead to Budget announcements

While the CGT decision provides certainty in one area, property owners should remain alert for other potential tax changes when the Chancellor delivers his Budget on 28 October. The Treasury may still introduce adjustments to property taxation through alternative measures.

Financial advisers recommend that landlords and investors review their portfolios in light of the confirmed CGT position, as those considering property sales might find the current tax regime more favourable than potential future changes. As always, seeking professional tax advice tailored to individual circumstances remains crucial when making significant financial decisions.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Recent developments in the UK property sector highlight significant leadership changes and strategic moves aimed at enhancing market expertise and lead generation. Two prominent estate agencies, Chestertons and Moveli, have announced key appointments that could reshape their operations in Central London and beyond.

Chestertons Promotes Andrew Chrysanthou to Regional Director

Chestertons has appointed Andrew Chrysanthou as the new regional director of Central London lettings. With over 15 years of experience in the property industry, Chrysanthou brings a wealth of knowledge to the role. He joined Chestertons nine years ago and has since played a pivotal part in the success of the agency’s Knightsbridge lettings business.

In his new position, Chrysanthou will oversee lettings teams across Central London, focusing on strengthening landlord relationships and driving business development. His career began as a negotiator in 2009, and prior to joining Chestertons, he held branch management roles at Cluttons and Barnard Marcus, covering areas such as Clapham, Fulham, and Earl’s Court.

Commenting on his promotion, Chrysanthou said, “Central London is a diverse market, and landlords and tenants value clear advice from professionals who understand their neighbourhoods. With tenant demand on the rise, I’m excited to work with our teams to build on their local expertise.”

Katinka Hill, head of lettings at Chestertons, praised Chrysanthou’s contributions, stating, “Andrew has been instrumental in the success of our Knightsbridge operations. His deep market knowledge and leadership skills make him the ideal candidate for this role.”

Moveli Appoints Tristan Redburn to Lead New Business Department

Meanwhile, Moveli has announced the appointment of Tristan Redburn to head its newly established business development department. Redburn joins Moveli after eight years at Hamptons, where he led a team that generated £12 million in revenue for the wider network.

Moveli, which recently surpassed 100 brokers, has launched this department to enhance lead generation and prospecting activities. The agency currently distributes over 100 seller leads monthly, and the new team aims to increase this figure through targeted prospecting and leveraging brokers’ existing client databases.

Redburn’s role will involve reconnecting with former clients, applicants, and valuation prospects to identify potential sellers. Brokers will retain control over their client relationships while benefiting from Moveli’s expanded lead generation capabilities. The agency also plans to integrate advanced technologies, including automation and AI, into its Moveli OS platform to streamline these processes.

Ben Littlewood, co-founder of Moveli, expressed confidence in Redburn’s appointment, highlighting his proven track record in business development and his ability to drive growth.

These strategic appointments reflect the evolving nature of the UK property market, with agencies investing in leadership and technology to meet growing demand and enhance client services. Homeowners and landlords may find these developments indicative of a more competitive and dynamic market landscape.

item.title: Estate agents demand housing market boost as Budget scepticism grows
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

As the Autumn Budget approaches, concerns are mounting among estate agents about the government’s ability to provide meaningful support for the UK housing market. Despite recent initiatives aimed at first-time buyers, a survey by GetAgent reveals that 84% of agents lack confidence in housing featuring prominently in the Budget. This scepticism comes amidst a challenging year for the property sector, with over half of agents (56%) reporting that the market has performed worse than expected in 2026.

Market Performance and Government Intervention

The survey highlights widespread dissatisfaction with current market conditions. While 37% of agents noted that activity has broadly matched expectations, only 7% reported a stronger performance. Furthermore, 58% of respondents believe that existing government measures have failed to improve the market, with just 12% considering them effective. This sentiment underscores calls for more substantial intervention, as 68% of agents argue that a government-led boost is needed to stimulate activity.

First-time buyers remain a key focus for agents, with 40% identifying this group as the most urgently in need of support. Landlords and property investors followed at 29%, while existing homeowners looking to move accounted for 14%. Tenants were prioritised by just 10% of respondents. In response to these concerns, the government recently announced the Your First Home scheme, which aims to assist first-time buyers in England by offering a deposit as low as 2.5% alongside a 20% government-backed equity loan.

Call for Broader Market Support

While the Your First Home scheme addresses one of the industry’s main concerns, questions remain about whether the Budget will include wider measures to support housing transactions. Colby Short, co-founder and CEO of GetAgent, acknowledged the announcement as a step in the right direction but emphasised the need for broader action. “The government has identified an area where agents believe intervention is most urgently needed,” he said. “However, agents clearly believe more needs to be done to stimulate the wider market.”

The property industry is calling for comprehensive measures that go beyond first-time buyer incentives. With market activity remaining subdued, agents are urging the government to implement strategies that will boost confidence and encourage transactions across all buyer groups. As the Budget announcement looms, the sector awaits clarity on whether policymakers will heed these calls.

With the housing market at a crossroads, the Autumn Budget presents a crucial opportunity for the government to address these concerns and introduce measures that could reinvigorate the property sector. Homeowners, buyers, and industry professionals alike will be watching closely to see if the Budget delivers the support needed to drive market activity forward.

item.title: Prime London rental yields hit 17-year high as landlords weigh their options
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Rental yields in prime central London have reached their highest level in over 15 years, according to recent data. Rising rents combined with softer property values are creating favourable conditions for landlords, particularly in the capital’s most sought-after locations. However, regulatory changes and tax pressures continue to weigh heavily on the sector, potentially impacting the availability of rental properties.

Prime London Rental Growth Accelerates

Figures from Savills indicate that prime central London rents increased by 1.1% in the third quarter of 2026, marking the strongest quarterly growth in two years. Over the past year, rents in this area have risen by 1.9%. Meanwhile, outer prime London saw a 0.9% quarterly increase, bringing annual rental inflation to 2.9%. This growth is partly driven by a reduction in rental supply, particularly for properties with annual rents below £100,000, which has intensified competition among tenants.

The Renters’ Rights Act, introduced in recent years, has been identified as a key concern for landlords. Nearly half of Savills’ agents highlighted the legislation as a significant issue, alongside increased taxation on property income and rising mortgage costs. These factors have led to heightened caution among landlords, with some reassessing their portfolios and, in some cases, exiting the market altogether.

Smaller Properties Deliver Stronger Yields

Smaller properties, particularly one-bedroom flats, are currently offering the highest rental yields in prime London. Gross yields for these apartments average 5.8%, while yields across prime London flats generally exceed 4%. This trend is attributed to rising rents and a decline in capital values, which have pushed average yields in prime central London to their highest level since 2009.

Despite these strong yields, landlords should be mindful of additional costs, such as higher mortgage rates, maintenance expenses, and compliance with regulatory requirements. These factors can erode net returns, even in a high-yield environment. For those considering retaining their rental properties, it could be worth seeking professional advice to navigate the complex landscape effectively.

Regional Rental Growth Remains Subdued

Outside London, prime rental growth has been far more modest. In the third quarter of 2026, average rents across prime regional markets increased by just 0.3%. This slower pace reflects broader economic pressures and a more balanced supply-demand dynamic in these areas. For landlords operating outside the capital, the focus may need to shift towards maximising occupancy and maintaining property appeal to attract tenants.

As the rental market continues to evolve, landlords might consider reviewing their strategies to adapt to changing conditions. Whether in prime London or regional markets, staying informed about regulatory developments and market trends could help ensure long-term success in the sector.

While higher yields in prime central London present opportunities, landlords must weigh these against the challenges of increased taxation and regulatory scrutiny. With careful planning and a proactive approach, property investors may find ways to navigate this complex landscape effectively.

item.title: Buy-to-let yields hit 15 year high
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Landlords across the UK may be encouraged by the latest figures showing buy-to-let yields reaching their highest level in 15 years. According to recent data, gross rental returns averaged 7.22% in the third quarter of 2026, marking a significant uptick in profitability for property investors. This trend highlights the potential for strong returns in the buy-to-let market, particularly for those considering specific property types or regions.

Regional Variations in Rental Returns

The East Midlands emerged as a standout performer, boasting an impressive average yield of 8.10%. This region’s strong performance suggests that landlords investing in this area could benefit from higher rental incomes relative to property prices. Meanwhile, houses in multiple occupation (HMOs) continued to deliver robust returns, with average yields reaching 8.80%. These figures indicate that HMOs remain a popular choice for investors seeking above-average rental yields.

What This Means for Buy-to-Let Investors

The rise in buy-to-let yields could signal a favourable period for property investors, particularly those looking to expand their portfolios. However, it’s worth noting that yields can vary significantly depending on factors such as location, property type, and market conditions. Landlords may wish to carefully assess their investment strategies to ensure they maximise returns whilst managing associated risks, such as maintenance costs and potential voids.

For those considering entering the buy-to-let market, these figures underscore the importance of thorough research and planning. Seeking professional advice and staying informed about regional trends could help investors make well-informed decisions. Additionally, exploring mortgage options tailored to buy-to-let properties may help secure competitive financing and enhance overall profitability.

As the buy-to-let market continues to evolve, these record-breaking yields highlight the potential for strong returns in certain sectors. Whether focusing on high-performing regions or specific property types, investors could find opportunities to achieve their financial goals in the current landscape.
